hints.content:
We can use Cavalieri's principle to show that two figures have the same volume if we establish:

- Their base areas are the same.
- They have the same cross-sectional area at any given point above their bases.
- Their heights are the same.

Let's go through Tim's work part by part and find the first mistake that he made.

###Base areas

> *"The base areas are the same."*

$\begin{align}
\text{area}_\text{rectangle} &= bh
\\\\
&=6 \cdot 2
\\\\
&=12
\\\\
\text{area}_\text{triangle} &= \dfrac12bh
\\\\
&=\dfrac12 \cdot 6 \cdot 4
\\\\
&=12
\end{align}$

Tim is correct here.

###Cross-sectional areas

> *"...corresponding cross-sections have the same area."*



[[☃ image 1]]

In each figure, the cross-sectional area is the base area. We know the base areas are the same, and this area stays the same at each height, so Tim is correct here.

options.alt: A rectangular prism and an oblique triangular prism. Both have the same number of cross sections.

hints.content:
###Heights

Tim didn't say anything about the heights being the same. Cavalieri's principle relies on this, since each figure needs to have the same number of layers when it comes to their cross-sections.
Tim did not establish that heights are the same.

question.content:
Consider the following rectangular-based and triangular-based prisms.



[[☃ image 1]]

Tim tried to use Cavalieri's principle to show that the two figures have the same volume.

> *"The base areas are the same. Therefore, corresponding cross-sections have the same area. So the volumes must be the same."*

**What is the first mistake Tim made?**

[[☃ radio 1]]

options.alt: A right rectangular prism and an oblique triangular prism that leans to the right at the top. The right rectangular prism has a length of six units, a width of two units, and a height of ten units. The base of the oblique triangular prism has a base of six units and a height of four units. One of the slanted edges of the oblique triangular prism has a length of eleven, but the oblique prism has a height of ten.

choices.content: The base areas are not the same.
It isn’t true that corresponding cross-sections have the same area.
He did not establish that heights are the same.
